lead: A casting does not freeze all at once. Heat leaves through the mould wall, so the metal near the wall freezes first and the freezing front moves inward. Pure metals freeze at one temperature; alloys freeze over a range and form a mushy zone. The zone pattern, directional solidification and three shrinkages decide whether the casting is sound. Chvorinov's rule turns this picture into a number: solidification time depends on volume divided by cooling surface area. Foundries use it to compare the freezing time of a casting with that of its riser.
prereq: You need: 1.1 for the mould and 1.4 for gating, risers and Chvorinov's rule.

blocks.text: Solidification begins with nucleation. The liquid metal must form stable solid nuclei before crystals can grow. Homogeneous nucleation means nuclei form inside the liquid itself; it needs high undercooling. Heterogeneous nucleation on the mould wall, on sand grains or on inclusions is easier and common in castings. Once nuclei exist, they grow by adding atoms from the liquid. Grains that grow fastest along the direction opposite to heat flow become long and columnar.

Three zones usually appear from the wall inward. The chill zone is a thin layer of fine equiaxed grains at the mould wall. The wall removes heat fast, so many nuclei survive and no grain grows large. Next is the columnar zone. These grains are long and roughly parallel to the heat flow, because the liquid ahead is cooler and growth along the steep temperature gradient wins. At the centre is the equiaxed zone: random, roughly equal-sized grains that form in the last liquid, often helped by added grain refiners.

Directional solidification means keeping this freezing front moving steadily toward the riser. Then each part of the casting freezes before the liquid feeding it is cut off. Chills, exothermic sleeves and a suitable temperature gradient help. Good directional solidification gives a sound casting; poor control leaves a mushy centre that cannot be fed. The figure shows the order from the mould wall to the centre.

sections.h3: Pure metals, alloys and three shrinkages

blocks.text: Pure metals and eutectic alloys freeze at a single temperature. The solid–liquid front is sharp. Alloys with a freezing range start freezing at the liquidus temperature and finish at the solidus temperature. Between these two temperatures, solid dendrites and liquid coexist in a mushy zone. A wide freezing range gives a long mushy zone. Liquid cannot flow easily through it, so feeding becomes difficult and small dispersed shrinkage pores can remain. A narrow range keeps the front tighter and easier to feed. Some syllabi call this solidification of alloys.

The three shrinkages are best kept separate. Liquid shrinkage is the volume decrease when liquid metal cools to its freezing point. Solidification shrinkage is the volume decrease when liquid becomes solid; most metals shrink on freezing, with grey cast iron a famous exception because graphite growth offsets it. Solid shrinkage is the volume decrease when the frozen solid cools to room temperature. A riser feeds liquid and solidification shrinkage; the pattern's shrinkage allowance compensates solid shrinkage. See 1.4 for riser sizing and 1.8 for shrinkage defects.

A freezing range also changes the zone structure. The mushy zone can block the columnar front, and equiaxed grains may grow inside it. That is why alloy castings often need grain refinement, chills and careful riser placement.
Chvorinov's rule is the working formula for solidification time. It compares castings made in the same mould from the same metal.

blocks.where: t is solidification time (s or min); V is casting volume; A is the heat-losing surface area; B is the mould constant for the metal and mould; n is the exponent, usually 2.

blocks.text: The rule is used as a ratio. If two castings have the same B and n, t₂/t₁ = [(V/A)₂/(V/A)₁]<sup>n</sup>. For a cube of side a, V = a³ and A = 6a², so V/A = a/6. Under the same conditions, a cube's solidification time scales with a², not a³. Doubling the side doubles the modulus and makes the time four times as large. The volume becomes eight times as large, but time does not. Use the rule to check that a riser freezes after the casting it feeds: the riser needs a larger modulus than the casting so it stays liquid while the casting freezes. The worked example applies the ratio to two cubes.

examples.question: A 200 mm cube casting solidifies in 20 min in a sand mould. Using Chvorinov's rule with n = 2, find the solidification time of a 100 mm cube of the same metal in the same mould.
steps: For a cube of side a, V = a³ and A = 6a², so V/A = a/6.
Chvorinov's rule: t = B (V/A)². With the same B, t₂/t₁ = [(V/A)₂/(V/A)₁]².
examples.answer: The 100 mm cube solidifies in 5.0 min.
examples.check:
side1 = 200
side2 = 100
t1 = 20
t2 = t1 * ((side2 / 6) / (side1 / 6)) ** 2
print(t2)

traps: Same shape, same mould: solidification time scales with the square of linear size, not with volume. A 100 mm cube takes one quarter of the 200 mm cube's time, not one eighth.
Do not use n = 3 for time just because volume goes as a³. Chvorinov's exponent is usually 2; V/A is a length, and the ratio uses (length ratio)^n.
Pure metals freeze at one temperature; alloys with a freezing range freeze between liquidus and solidus. A mushy zone is not the same as the columnar zone.
The chill zone is fine equiaxed grains at the wall. Columnar grains are long and point inward along heat flow; equiaxed grains at the centre are random.
A riser feeds liquid and solidification shrinkage. Solid shrinkage after freezing is handled by pattern shrinkage allowance, not by the riser.

quiz.q: Name the three grain zones from the mould wall to the centre of a casting.
quiz.a: Chill zone (fine equiaxed grains at the wall), columnar zone (long grains pointing inward), equiaxed zone (random grains at the centre).

quiz.q: Why do columnar grains grow inward in a casting?
quiz.a: Heat leaves through the mould wall, so the steepest temperature gradient and fastest growth are opposite to heat flow; grains that grow that way outrun others and form long columns.

quiz.q: A 150 mm cube solidifies in 36 min. Using Chvorinov's rule with n = 2, find the time for a 50 mm cube of the same metal in the same mould.
Why can a wide freezing-range alloy show dispersed porosity even with a riser?
quiz.a: The long mushy zone blocks liquid feeding; liquid cannot reach the last solidifying pockets, so small shrinkage pores remain scattered instead of one pipe.

quiz.q: Define liquid shrinkage, solidification shrinkage and solid shrinkage.
quiz.a: Liquid shrinkage: volume decrease while liquid cools to freezing point. Solidification shrinkage: volume decrease when liquid turns solid. Solid shrinkage: volume decrease when solid cools to room temperature.

quiz.q: What is directional solidification and why is it used?
quiz.a: It keeps the freezing front moving toward the riser, so liquid metal can feed each region before it freezes. It reduces shrinkage porosity and makes the casting sound.

quiz.q: A casting has V/A = 30 mm and its riser has V/A = 45 mm. Same mould and metal, n = 2. Which freezes first, and what is the ratio of riser time to casting time?
quiz.a: t ∝ (V/A)². Casting modulus is smaller, so casting freezes first. t_riser/t_casting = (45/30)² = (1.5)² = 2.25; the riser takes 2.25 times longer.

beyond: Not for the exam. Foundries now simulate the freezing front with software that solves heat flow and alloy solidification, then predict porosity before a mould is cut. Thermal analysis of the cooling curve is used on the shop floor to check melt quality and grain refinement. Additive manufacturing of sand moulds lets designers place chills and channels that were costly in a conventional pattern. Search next for 'casting simulation', 'thermal analysis of cast iron' and 'directional solidification'.
